panels.figure_caption: Radiographic findings in two pediatric patients diagnosed with cystinuria. (A) Renal ultrasound of Case 1: The kidneys are normal in size and position. In the right kidney, there are subcentimeter calculi at the upper and lower poles, each measuring up to 4 mm (indicated as 1 and 2). In the left kidney, a 3 mm nonobstructing calculus is seen at the lower pole (data not shown). No hydronephrosis or hydroureter is present. (B) Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (Case 2): A 3.5 cm staghorn calculus is seen extending from the mid to lower pole of the right kidney into the renal pelvis. No ureteral or left-sided calculi are identified.
in_text_mentions: In the renal clinic, her serum creatinine and kidney function were within normal limits. However, 24 h urine studies showed hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia. Potassium citrate therapy was initiated along with recommendations for increased oral fluid intake and dietary sodium restriction. Despite these measures, the patient continued to experience symptoms and underwent two surgical interventions for left ureterolithiasis and left ureteral calculi. Follow-up renal ultrasound showed persistent non-obstructing renal stones measuring 3–4 mm (Figure 1A).

She was subsequently evaluated in urology after being discharged from the ED. A repeat non-contrast CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.5 cm staghorn calculus occupying the mid to lower pole of the right kidney, extending into the renal pelvis (Figure 1B). Her basic metabolic panel and other laboratory studies were within normal limits. Stone analysis determined 100% cystine composition. She was referred to nephrology for further evaluation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial non-contrast CT of a real patient (case report of cystinuria with a 49-year diagnostic delay) showing left renal calculi with hydronephrosis, a captioned, disease-specific manifestation of cystinuria-related urolithiasis. Hydronephrosis is in the vocabulary; the renal calculus itself is proposed since no CT-specific renal calculus key exists. B: Coronal non-contrast CT of the same patient showing a left renal calculus with hydronephrosis; captioned disease-specific manifestation of cystinuria. C: Axial non-contrast CT of a real patient showing a left proximal ureteric calculus, a captioned manifestation matching the cystinuria ureteral calculus vocabulary key in this cystinuria case report. D: Coronal non-contrast CT of the same patient showing multiple proximal left ureteric calculi, a captioned disease-specific manifestation of cystinuria-related stone disease.

in_text_mentions: Noncontrast CT imaging of the urinary tract identified left renal calculi and multiple proximal ureteric stones, measuring up to 9.5 mm in diameter, accompanied by hydronephrosis (Figure 1). Average stone density was calculated as 650 Hounsfield units. Radiological imaging provided no evidence of right‐sided renal or ureteric calculi. The patient underwent emergency rigid cystoscopy and placement of a left JJ stent to decompress the urinary system. He was discharged the following day with plans for definitive stone surgery at a later date.

in_text_mentions: mL/min/1.73m2. CT scan showed multiple stones of the left kidney in the lower and middle calyces and cast stones in the lower columns and pyelon. The right kidney was hypotrophic with lobulated contour, signs of post-inflammation changes, and multiple mineral stones along with the previously placed double J stent (Figures 1, 2). Treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics and hydration was commenced. The right double J stent was replaced and another double J stent was placed in the left kidney. Following treatment, the kidney function started to improve along with a fall in inflammatory markers.

panels.rationale: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT of a human patient with congenital cystinuria and recurrent nephrolithiasis, showing an annotated right lower calyceal calculus (red crosshair, x:284, y:328, HU:729) matching the caption's 10 × 6 mm stone with ~742 HU attenuation; in-text also reports an additional 2.7 mm right lower pole calculus and bilateral punctate corticomedullary calcifications/nephrocalcinosis, supporting the multiple-calculi finding of cystinuria. Real patient radiology image, no third-party copyright indicated; no skin, ethnicity or age data available.
panels.attribution_text: Mazumder et al. Recurrent Nephrolithiasis in Congenital Cystinuria With a Complete Duplex Collecting System: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112780. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT scan showing a right lower calyceal stone measuring 10 × 6 mm, with a CT attenuation of approximately 742 Hounsfield units (HU). Although non-contrast CT is the standard imaging modality for urolithiasis, contrast-enhanced CT was performed in this patient to better delineate the complex renal collecting system anatomy, given the known duplex ureter and the extensive history of prior urological interventions [2]. Contrast imaging aided in procedural planning and the assessment of the collecting system prior to management.
in_text_mentions: A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 10 × 6 mm calculus within the right lower calyx with a CT attenuation of approximately 742 Hounsfield units (HU). An additional smaller calculus measuring 2.7 mm was noted in the right renal lower pole with a CT density of 283 HU. Multiple bilateral punctate calcifications at the corticomedullary junction were also observed, suggestive of nephrocalcinosis (Figure 1).

During the initial URS procedure, the right ureter was found to be tight, rendering it unsafe to proceed with flexible ureterorenoscopy due to the significant risk of ureteric injury. Consequently, a DJ stent was inserted in the right lower moiety. The subsequent attempt at flexible ureterorenoscopy and laser lithotripsy was unsuccessful, as the complete fragmentation of the stone could not be achieved due to these anatomical difficulties (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial non-contrast CT panel from a kidney transplant recipient shows a large 49 mm, 690 HU calculus in the renal allograft. The article title and in-text state acquired cystinuria and >95% cystine stone composition, supporting attribution to cystinuria/cystine urolithiasis. The setting is atypical. b: Coronal non-contrast CT panel from the same kidney transplant recipient shows the large 49 mm, 690 HU cystine calculus in the renal allograft. The article title and in-text support acquired cystinuria with >95% cystine stone composition; the transplant/acquired setting is atypical.
panels.attribution_text: Martin et al. Acquired cystinuria in a kidney transplant recipient.. Clinical kidney journal 2025. doi:10.1093/ckj/sfaf330. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1:.
panels.figure_caption: Abdominal NCCT, showing a complex stone of 49 mm in diameter, 690 HU density in the lower calyx of the renal allograft. (a) Axial section. (b) Coronal section.
in_text_mentions: At 6 years post-transplantation, a CT-scan performed for an adrenal adenoma fortuitously revealed a complex stone of 49 mm in diameter and 690 Hounsfield unit (HU) density, without pyelocaliceal dilation (Fig. 1). Routine annual kidney ultrasounds were reviewed, without evidence for urolithiasis. A mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) allowed complete fragmentation and drainage of the calculus. Infrared spectrophotometric analysis confirmed that the stones contained >95% of cystine.
